newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai stocks to climb, but rally seen limited.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai stocks to climb, but rally seen limited.

text.p: Profit taking is set to cap a fierce rally in Thai stocks near-term, but the outlook for the battered bourse has brightened since the baht's flotation, traders and brokers said on Friday.
The central bank ended months of devaluation speculation on Wednesday by floating the currency to help pull Thailand out of its biggest economic slump for more than a decade.
The move saw the baht lose around 15-20 percent of its value in offshore markets, but sparked a stampede for Thai stocks which allowed the market to leap from near eight year lows.
The SET Index closed on Thursday at 617.98, a 90.70 point or 17.20 percent, rise over the two trading days since the baht was floated. It rose 7.99 percent to 667.36 at Friday's open.
With most blue chips hitting their daily 10 percent trading limits within minutes of opening, investors have been rushing into any available vehicle with which to ride the rally.
Prices on the no-limits foreign board of shares have rocketed 200-300 percent to levels not seen since July 1995.
"It shows that everyone agrees that you buy after a devaluation and not before. There has been a frantic scramble for stock," said Ian Mclennan, head of research at SBC Warburg.

A backlog of orders and continued buying by offshore fund managers allowed the domestic market to soar again on Friday morning. But some prices look overstretched and profit taking may help cap the rally at around 650, analysts said.

For many corporations, the de facto devaluation will wipe out earnings this year and trigger a spate of defaults caused by the rising costs of repayments on unhedged foreign denominated loans, analysts said.
But the baht's managed float lifts prospects of a long term recovery in the economy and a gradually rising market, they said.
Economic growth may slow to around 3-4 percent this year from 6.4 in 1996, but forecasts predict exports wil rise by around 10 percent.
Many analysts also believe that Thai interest rates, among the highest in the region, may start to fall in 1998.
Jim Landi head of research at Vickers Ballas, said interest rates may fall by between 200-300 basis points next year if the baht stays stable and capital inflows improve liquidity.

"We are going to have some short term pain but it looks like the way is clear for a pretty good recovery in economic fundamentals and that would be the basis for having a sustained market rally ... perhaps to around 800 by year end" Landi said.

While the near-term outlook remains volatile and prospects for many struggling firms bleak, the market may now offer long term gains in stocks of companies with solid fundamentals and which are hedged against currency fluctuations, analysts said.
"I think in the longer term in the next few months we are going to hear an awful lot about defaults and confidence is going to remain low," Mclennan said.
"But ... the index should be gradually climbing, though it will be climbing a wall of fear. It is still a bit early, but I think generally this could be the turning point," he said.
